reference.source: Diving and aviation medicine / dental references
clinicalPearls: Tooth pain provoked by changes in ambient pressure during flying or diving
It is almost always a symptom of pre-existing dental pathology rather than a disease in itself
Underlying causes include caries, defective restorations, pulpitis, periapical disease and recent dental work
Pain classically occurs on ascent in flight or on descent when diving, as trapped gas expands or contracts
Severe dental barotrauma can rarely cause tooth or restoration fracture
Prevention rests on maintaining dental health and deferring diving or flying after certain dental procedures
reference.pathophysiology: Barodontalgia arises when ambient pressure changes act on gas trapped within a tooth or its surrounding tissues, or when pressure change stimulates a diseased or inflamed pulp. According to Boyle's law, gas trapped beneath a restoration or within carious or periapical spaces expands as pressure falls and contracts as it rises, producing pain, while an already inflamed pulp becomes sensitive to these changes. The pain is therefore a manifestation of underlying dental disease unmasked by the pressure environment.
additionalDifferentials: Maxillary sinus barotrauma referring pain to upper teeth
Pulpitis or periapical disease unrelated to pressure
Referred pain from other orofacial pathology
additionalInvestigations: Dental examination and imaging to identify the underlying pathology
History correlating pain with ascent or descent
Exclusion of sinus barotrauma as a source of referred pain
Vitality testing of the implicated tooth
redFlags: Severe pain with in-flight or in-water incapacitation risk
Evidence of tooth or restoration fracture
Recurrent episodes indicating untreated dental disease
reference.prognosis: The symptom resolves once the underlying dental problem is treated, and prevention is effective with good dental care and appropriate timing of diving or flying after dental work.
pitfalls: Treating the pain without identifying and managing the underlying dental disease
Confusing referred sinus barotrauma pain with true barodontalgia
Clearing personnel to dive or fly with untreated dental pathology
Overlooking recent dental work as a precipitant
references: Diving and aviation medicine references (standard reference)
management: Definitive treatment of the underlying dental pathology, such as restoration of caries or replacement of defective restorations
Root canal treatment for pulpitis and management of periapical disease, with extraction of non-restorable teeth
Analgesia for symptomatic relief pending definitive dental care
Deferral of diving or flying for an appropriate interval after dental procedures until healing is complete
Exclusion and treatment of sinus barotrauma as a source of referred pain
Preventive dental care and regular review to maintain barometric fitness
Referral to dental or diving and aviation medicine services for fitness-to-dive or fitness-to-fly assessment
